analysis.one_liner: Requires employers with 15 or more workers to provide seven days of paid sick leave a year.
analysis.headline: The first national paid sick leave bill drew 71 cosponsors but was sent to a House subcommittee and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every employer with 15 or more employees to give workers at least seven paid sick days a year to recover from illness, see a doctor, or care for a sick child, spouse, or parent, with a prorated amount for part-time workers. Workers with generous existing leave would keep it, and employers could not take away leave to comply. It never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly the tens of millions of workers at 15-plus-employee businesses who had no paid sick leave — concentrated among low-income workers, of whom 76 percent of the poorest families lacked it. The bill let them stay home when sick, take a child to the doctor, or get preventive care without losing pay or their job.

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers with 15 or more employees to provide seven days of paid sick leave annually for full-time workers, and a prorated amount for workers averaging at least 20 hours a week or 1,000 hours a year.
The leave can be used for the worker's own illness or medical care, or to care for a child, parent, spouse, or other close family member.

Employers cannot interfere with the right to take leave, count sick days against workers under no-fault attendance policies, or fire or retaliate against workers who use the leave; workers can sue and recover lost wages plus damages, and the Labor Department can investigate and enforce.
Employers with existing equivalent paid-leave policies would not have to change them, and the bill bars employers from cutting existing leave to comply.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees, who would bear the cost of up to seven days of paid leave per worker per year plus recordkeeping and compliance; the cost falls hardest on industries that rely on hourly workers, and employers might respond with slower hiring or higher prices.

drawbacks.text: The mandate is a real cost to employers, who must pay wages for days not worked; businesses near the 15-employee threshold could face pressure to hold hiring below it, and industries that employ many hourly workers would bear the largest share.

The bill requires a doctor's certification for any leave longer than three consecutive days, which adds a hurdle — and a cost — for workers without health insurance, a gap the bill only directs regulators to work out later.
The bill's cost estimates and effects on small employers were never studied in committee, so no formal congressional assessment of the burden exists in the record.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers without any paid sick leave, seven paid days a year is a substantial protection — it means seeing a doctor or staying home with a sick child without losing income or risking a job. The main cost is borne by employers, and the bill softens it with prorated leave for part-timers, equivalency for firms with generous policies, and a ban on cutting existing leave. The honest unknown is how much of the cost employers would pass on through prices or slower hiring; the record contains no committee analysis of that, because the bill never got that far.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees, then sent to the Workforce Protections subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Healthy Families Act on April 27, 2005, the first bill to establish a national paid sick leave requirement.
It drew 71 cosponsors — 70 House Democrats and 1 Independent — all from one party.
The bill was referred to the Education and the Workforce, Government Reform, and House Administration committees on the day it was introduced.
On May 17, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where it remained for the rest of the 109th Congress with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have had to provide paid sick leave were better off, because the bill never reached a vote and no requirement took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have paid for leave

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led 43 original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: 71 House cosponsors (70 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: John Boehner
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired never reported the bill or scheduled a markup; it was sent to a subcommittee and never moved again.

against.name: Subcommittee on Workforce Protections
against.role: House Education and the Workforce subcommittee of jurisdiction
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 17, 2005, and took no action for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 71 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent; the bill was referred to committees controlled by the House Republican majority and never advanced.

industries.industry: Employers of hourly and service workers (retail, food service, hospitality)
industries.note: These employers would have paid up to seven days of wages per worker per year, and they employ most of the workers who lacked sick leave. Their cost under the bill is the direct benefit to those workers.
The bill anticipated that paid leave would let workers get earlier, routine care instead of delaying treatment or using emergency rooms, increasing use of preventive and primary care.
